title: CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27 | CBC News
html:
Business

CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27

Bell faces a fine of up to $10M for selling locked mobile devices

Canada's telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.

At the same time, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has threatened Bell with a fine of up to $10 million for violating the government's wireless rules by selling customers cellphones locked to its network.

The CRTC's decision targets charges for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan. The regulator ruled on Friday that a cellphone handling charge from Bell, a cellphone setup charge from Rogers and a SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from Telus are prohibited.

The CRTC also ruled that fees charged by Rogers and Telus to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, nor are the shipping fees charged by Rogers.

SIM cards are microchips needed to connect a customer's device to a mobile network.

In June, the regulator banned fees to activate, change or cancel internet and cellphone services. Following that ban, major carriers introduced SIM card and other hardware-related charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees.

"We identified a number of fees charged by certain of the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. We notified them that the fees may be out of compliance," Sheehan Carter, the CRTC's acting vice-president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing on Friday.

"Since these companies chose to continue those fees, and they argued that they were not prohibited, we immediately took action to decide the issue."

In a statement to CBC News on Friday, Rogers said it disagrees with the CRTC's position on device set-up charges.

"These charges help recover real costs, and we're pleased the CRTC's decision on the shipping charge and SIM replacement fee clearly reflect this," a Rogers spokesperson told CBC News in an email.

Spokespeople for Bell and Telus say their respective companies are reviewing the regulator's decisions.

According to a CRTC report released in February, Bell, Telus and Rogers collectively controlled nearly 90 per cent of Canada's mobile wireless sales and roughly 86 per cent of wireless subscribers, as of 2024.

Matt Hatfield, executive director of the non-profit advocacy group OpenMedia, says Friday's ruling blocks some anti-consumer practices adopted by Canada's three largest telecom providers. However, he worries they will simply tweak their fees again to get around the rules.

"This is just one round of whack-a-mole in a game customers always lose. Canada's telecom companies keep finding new ways to lock in and surcharge their customers," he told CBC News in an emailed statement.

"As it stands, these practices were a net win for the companies. They profited while they lasted, and they'll now start on new ways of abusing customers that the CRTC will take time to identify and address."

Bell faces up to $10M fine

The CRTC also said Friday it found that Bell sold customers cellphones that were locked to its network — limiting their ability to take advantage of better offers from rivals.

"The CRTC rules require that cellphones must be unlocked, so that Canadians have the freedom to choose their provider," Carter said.

He said the CRTC is considering fining Bell up to $10 million, in the "upper range" of what's allowed under the Telecommunications Act. Earlier this month, BCE, Bell's parent company, booked $6.18 billion in operating revenue for the three months ending Sept. 30.

The CRTC banned phone locking in 2017, along with the unlocking fees carriers had been charging, in a bid to make it easier for consumers to switch providers.

In August, the CRTC temporarily suspended this requirement, allowing carriers to lock devices for up to two business days, after which they unlock automatically. It required that consumers be able to request immediate unlocking at no charge. This followed applications from Bell and Telus, which argued that selling unlocked phones increased theft and fraud.

In July, Telus filed an application for a temporary exemption from the regulator's phone-unlocking rules. The company proposed to start locking devices for 60 days.

On Friday, the CRTC formally denied this request.

Carter said the regulator had seen no evidence that Telus had actually sold locked devices, only that it intended to do so. As a result, he said no fines were appropriate at this time.

In June, the CRTC warned Telus in a letter that its $15 charge for SIM cards may be considered an activation fee, which is prohibited under the Telecommunications Act.

"Every SIM card and eSIM comes with real costs associated with providing it to customers, and we believe those costs should be reflected in the price of the product, rather than requiring carriers to provide it free of charge," a Telus spokesperson stated in an email.

Keldon Bester, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Monopoly Project, sees charges for SIM cards as an activation fee in disguise.

"You really cannot access telecom services without access to a SIM card," he said. "To break that out as a separate charge, I think, runs in the face of the CRTC's aim, which is to say that the process of moving carriers should be as seamless as possible."
summary: Canada's telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.
